newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rubin tells Japan not to let surplus surge.
newsitem.headline: Rubin tells Japan not to let surplus surge.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin urged Japan on Friday to guard against a resurgence of its trade surplus, but rejected suggestions that a stronger Japanese currency was the best way to do that.
Rubin told the American Chamber of Commerce here that Japan needed to promote strong domestic demand for its products, open up its markets further to imports and deregulate its economy.

"It is critical that Japan's current account surplus not rise again to a level that is detrimental to global growth, that causes trade friction with Japan's trading partners and that could fuel protectionist sentiments," he told the business leaders after meeting Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Japan's trade surplus rose in February for the first time in two years, as the weak yen helped make the nation's exports more competitive in world markets.
Speaking to reporters on his way here, Rubin made clear that he did not see a stronger yen -- and by inference a weaker dollar -- as the best way to contain and cut Japan's surplus.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," he said.

U.S. business leaders, however, made clear to Rubin that they were concerned about the weakness of the yen -- which has fallen some 50 percent against the dollar over the past two years, boosting Japanese competitiveness in the process.
"At current exchange rates, our profitability here is being killed," Robert Orr, director of government relations for Nippon Motorola Ltd, told Rubin.
Rubin has consistently maintained that a strong dollar is in America's interests -- a stance he alluded to on Friday -- because it keeps down U.S. inflation and interest rates.
But he has also recently taken to saying that the U.S. currency has been strong for some time, in an apparent effort to signal that he is not eager to see a further dollar advance.
The dollar did rise on Friday, jumping more than one yen to 123.79 yen in late Asian trade, as the market took Rubin's remarks to mean he would not actively push for a stronger yen.

Publicly, Rubin appeared willing to give Japan the benefit of the doubt -- for now -- that its policy gamble of mixing fiscal tightening with promised deregulation could achieve growth without relying on an export drive.
Some U.S. officials are worried that a rise in Japan's sales tax that took effect this week will sap demand at home and force Japanese companies to seek bigger profits overseas.

"I don't think there is any question...about his (Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto) commitment to deregulation and economic growth in Japan. It strikes me as a very sound policy path to be on," Rubin told a news conference.
But Rubin reserved judgment as to whether Japan's policy would succeed. "Only time will tell," he said.
The Treasury chief warned that Washington and other trade partners had "enormous interest" in how Japan's economy fared and whether Tokyo would act if its policy gamble failed.
Japanese officials said Hashimoto agreed with Rubin at their half-hour meeting that domestic demand-led growth was important for Japan, as it was for the United States.
Hashimoto repeated Japanese assurances that Tokyo's surplus was unlikely to grow drastically and that the economic impact from the consumption tax rise would be limited.
Looking back over the past four years, Rubin said that both the United States and Japan had worked hard to iron out trade friction and strengthen their economic relationship.
He noted that Japan's current account surplus -- the broadest measure of trade -- has fallen from the equivalent of 3.1 percent of gross domestic product in 1993 to 1.4 percent.

Four years ago, Washington tried unsuccessfully to convince Tokyo to adopt a surplus target of one-and-a-half to two percent of gross domestic product. But Rubin said on Friday that Washington did not have a target for the surplus now.

His visit to Japan follows a series of trips to Tokyo by U.S. officials including Vice President Al Gore and Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers. But Rubin denied there was a concerted U.S. strategy to turn up the heat on Japan.
Rubin was to leave Tokyo later on Friday for a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers in the Philippines.
